summary: Defines a header field that lets the author of an email or netnews message include a Jabber ID, tying the author to an XMPP address.

plainLanguage.summary: This adds a line to an email that says here is my chat address, so people can reach you in another way.

questions: how to put xmpp address in email header
subtitle: Add your XMPP chat address to an email message header.

tldr.problem: Email and netnews users who also use XMPP instant messaging want to advertise their XMPP address in their messages so others can contact them via chat.
tldr.mechanism: The Jabber-ID header field lets an email or netnews message author include a Jabber ID (an XMPP address) in the message header, following the same rules as other header fields.
tldr.outcome: Email clients and netnews readers that recognize the header can offer to start an XMPP chat with the author, or show whether they are online.

today: RFC 7259 is an Informational RFC that standardizes a header field the XMPP community had been using experimentally. The header is registered with IANA as a provisional header field.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
XMPP (the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol) is a real-time chat and presence system that grew out of the Jabber open-source project. XMPP addresses are still called Jabber IDs. Many people use both email and XMPP instant messaging, and this RFC lets them link the two by adding a Jabber ID header field to email and netnews messages.

The XMPP community has used the Jabber-ID header field informally for years. This document standardizes its syntax and usage so email and netnews clients can recognize it consistently.
sections.plainLanguage: Many people use both email and XMPP chat. This standard lets them put their XMPP address in an email so others know how to reach them via chat.

sections.title: The Jabber-ID Header Format
sections.content:
The Jabber-ID header field contains a single XMPP address (also called a pathxmpp). The header follows standard email header syntax from RFC 5322.

XMPP addresses can contain Unicode characters, but email and netnews headers allow only ASCII. Before including a Jabber ID in an email header, any non-ASCII characters must be converted using the rules in the XMPP URI specification (RFC 5122). This involves percent-encoding characters the same way URLs do. For example, an XMPP address with accented letters would be percent-encoded: ji%C5%99i@%C4%8Dechy.example instead of the original Unicode form.
sections.plainLanguage: The header just contains your XMPP address. If your address has special characters, they get converted to a form that works in email headers.

sections.title: Adding and Using the Header
sections.content:
The Jabber-ID header is associated with the author of the message. If an email's From: field lists multiple mailboxes, it is best not to add a Jabber-ID header, since it is unclear which author it belongs to. It is also recommended to include only one Jabber-ID header per message.

When a user agent receives an email or netnews message with a Jabber-ID header, it can convert any percent-encoded characters back to Unicode, yielding a valid XMPP address for the user's XMPP client. An email or netnews client that knows about the header can then show interface elements such as an indicator of whether the author is online (if the client is subscribed to their presence in XMPP) or a button to send an instant message.
sections.plainLanguage: When your email client sees the header, it can show you whether the person is online on XMPP and offer a button to send them a message.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Like all email headers, a Jabber-ID header can be forged. Applications should not depend on it to verify that a message is authentic or that the stated author is genuine.

Including a Jabber ID in email or netnews headers makes XMPP addresses visible and easier to harvest for spam. Combining an email address with a Jabber ID also makes it easier to link different kinds of communications traffic for surveillance. Email and netnews clients that include the Jabber-ID header should let users disable it globally, per recipient, or per message.

The security and privacy considerations in RFC 3986, RFC 3987, RFC 5122, RFC 6120, and RFC 6121 also apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Putting your XMPP address in email means anyone who reads your email can see it and might send you spam. It also links your email to your chat account, which could be a privacy issue. You should be able to turn it off.
